pages.text: Loose stone lies where the ground is bare. In places, the bones of the land break through the grass entirely.$(br2)Bare hands do nothing to a rock face. Something heavy, round and fist-sized does a great deal.
Pay attention to what comes off a worked face. Now and then the stone gives up a piece that sits in the hand as if it had always meant to be held.$(br2)Some seams are rarer, and better, than others.

$(l)Basalt$() is lava that cooled: dark, heavy and fine-grained, a tier behind chert. It lies scattered for forty blocks around lava - out in the open, and down in caves - thinning out as you go.$(br2)So a scatter of dark cobbles is a sign. Follow it in: where lava ran and cooled fast it went to glass, and $(#b87333)obsidian$() lies at the lava's edge.

Now and then an outcrop has a vein of $(#b87333)obsidian$() in its foot - three or four blocks of black glass at the bottom, where it meets the ground. Strike it like any face: a piece of glass each time. Ground with glass in it is worth more than any chert, and bands know it.

$(l)Gravel$() is worth sifting: sneak-use it with your hands free. Chert, often; now and then $(l)fine chert$() - glassier and redder than any seam gives, and keener; rarely obsidian that washed a long way; and once in a long while a whole $(l)chunk$() of it. Each patch is worth two goes.

An $(l)obsidian chunk$() is no hammerstone - strike with it and it bursts. It is the core an obsidian Levallois hand axe is struck from: lay it out among the stone at the station. Break it down for eight pieces. Or throw it, and watch it burst on whatever it hits.

Fine chert is in the living rock too, if you look: a block or two in the foot of a chert outcrop, now and then, and loose pieces of it weathered out round the edge. Very rarely a small seam of it stands on its own. Break a chunk of obsidian down by using it twice, quickly - it does not come apart by accident.
